questions.q: The largest earthwork at Cahokia, a platform mound whose base covers about 14 acres, is known by what name?
questions.explain: Monks Mound, named for Trappist monks who lived nearby in the 1800s, is the largest prehistoric earthen structure in the Americas north of Mexico.

questions.q: At Cahokia, archaeologists found circles of large wooden posts, nicknamed Woodhenge. What purpose are they thought to have served?
options: Fortifying the edge of the central plaza
Drying fish and meat for winter storage
Holding up the roof of a great council house
Marking solstices and equinoxes by the sun's position
questions.explain: Sunrise lined up with certain posts at the solstices and equinoxes, so the circles likely worked as solar calendars for ceremonies and planting.

questions.q: Poverty Point in Louisiana, a set of huge concentric earthen ridges built more than 3,000 years ago, is remarkable because its builders were mainly what?
options: Maize farmers who had migrated from Mesoamerica
Seafaring traders from the Caribbean islands
Herders of domesticated llamas and alpacas
questions.explain: UNESCO notes that Poverty Point's earthworks were built by hunter-fisher-gatherers, one of the largest such feats by a non-farming society anywhere.

questions.q: What is the name of the largest great house in Chaco Canyon, a D-shaped Ancestral Puebloan building that held hundreds of rooms?
questions.explain: Pueblo Bonito was built in stages from the mid-800s to the 1100s and rose four or five stories in places, making it the center of the Chaco world.

questions.q: Spiro Mounds, a Mississippian site in present-day Oklahoma, is famous for what discovery?
options: A burial mound filled with engraved shell, copper and textiles
A walled town of adobe apartment blocks
A stone calendar carved by visiting Maya scribes
The oldest known maize cobs in North America
questions.explain: Spiro's Craig Mound held a hollow 'Great Mortuary' rich in shell, copper and cloth from distant places; looters dug much of it out in the 1930s.

questions.q: Haudenosaunee tradition credits the Peacemaker and which partner, a grieving leader, with persuading five nations to accept the Great Law of Peace?
questions.explain: Hiawatha (Ayenwatha) carried the Peacemaker's message; the Onondaga chief Tadodaho resisted longest before the League was formed.

questions.q: The name Haudenosaunee, which the Iroquois use for themselves, means what?
questions.explain: The name pictures the league as one great longhouse stretching across New York; the Seneca were 'keepers of the western door.'

questions.q: Which waterfall, for thousands of years one of the great salmon-fishing and trading places of the Pacific Northwest, was flooded by The Dalles Dam in 1957?
questions.explain: Wasco, Wishram and other peoples fished salmon at Celilo Falls and hosted traders from far away; The Dalles Dam drowned the falls in 1957.

questions.q: The Chinook peoples, who lived where the great river of the Northwest meets the Pacific, were known for what role in the regional economy?
options: Trading as go-betweens for coastal and inland peoples
Raising bison in fenced river pastures
questions.explain: Living where the Columbia met the Pacific, the Chinook traded dried salmon, shells, canoes and slaves among peoples up and down the coast and inland.

questions.q: The Inca kept census and tribute records using what system?
options: Strings of shell beads called wampum
questions.explain: Quipu-keepers recorded numbers by the type and position of knots on hanging cords, letting the Inca run a large empire without a writing system.

questions.q: In 1532, Francisco Pizarro's small force captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa at which town?
questions.explain: Atahualpa paid a room full of gold and silver as ransom but was executed in 1533; Lima was founded by Pizarro only in 1535.

questions.q: When the Spanish arrived in Peru, Inca power had just been weakened by a civil war between Atahualpa and which half-brother?
questions.explain: Atahualpa had defeated Huascar shortly before Pizarro arrived, leaving the empire divided; Huascar was killed on Atahualpa's orders in 1532.

questions.q: On the 'Noche Triste' of 1520, what happened to the Spanish forces led by Cortes?
options: They captured Moctezuma inside his palace
They suffered heavy losses fleeing Tenochtitlan at night
They burned their ships to prevent desertion
They landed on the Gulf coast at Veracruz
questions.explain: After the Aztecs rose against them, the Spaniards and their allies tried to slip out along a causeway and lost hundreds of men and much treasure.

questions.q: Which Native city-state, a longtime enemy of the Aztecs, became the most important ally of the Spanish in the conquest of Tenochtitlan?
questions.explain: Thousands of Tlaxcalan warriors fought beside the Spanish, and Tlaxcala later won special privileges from the Spanish crown for its help.

questions.q: The Aztec Empire was formally a Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan and which two other city-states?
questions.explain: The alliance formed in 1428; over time Tenochtitlan became the dominant partner and collected most of the tribute.

questions.q: Who was the last Aztec ruler, captured when Tenochtitlan fell to the Spanish and their Native allies in August 1521?
questions.explain: Cuauhtemoc led the defense during the long siege; Cortes later had him executed in 1525 during an expedition to Honduras.

questions.q: Esteban, an enslaved man from Morocco who had survived the Narvaez expedition, was killed in 1539 while guiding a search for what?
options: A water passage to the Pacific
questions.explain: Esteban scouted ahead of Fray Marcos de Niza and died at the Zuni town of Hawikuh; the friar's report then inspired Coronado's 1540 expedition.

questions.q: Members of Coronado's expedition in 1540 became the first Europeans known to see which natural feature?
questions.explain: Hopi guides led a party under Garcia Lopez de Cardenas to the canyon rim, but the men could not find a way down to the river.

questions.q: After the Zuni towns disappointed him, Coronado pushed onto the Plains in 1541 seeking a rich land called Quivira. What did it turn out to be?
options: Grass-house villages of the Wichita in present-day Kansas
The abandoned city of Cahokia on the Mississippi
A silver-mining town in northern Mexico
A Pueblo town built of gold in Colorado
questions.explain: Instead of gold, Coronado found farming villages of the ancestors of the Wichita and returned to Mexico in 1542 a disappointed man.

questions.q: In 1565, Pedro Menendez de Aviles attacked which French Huguenot settlement near present-day Jacksonville, Florida?
questions.explain: Menendez captured Fort Caroline and executed most of the French prisoners, ending France's attempt to plant a colony in Florida.

questions.q: Tristan de Luna's 1559 attempt to plant a Spanish colony at what is now Pensacola Bay failed largely because of what?
options: A hurricane that wrecked most of the fleet soon after arrival
A mutiny led by sailors from Portugal
A smallpox epidemic among the colonists
questions.explain: The storm sank most ships and much of the food just weeks after landing; the colony struggled on and was abandoned in 1561.

questions.q: Jacques Cartier applied the name Canada to the St. Lawrence region after hearing an Iroquoian word meaning what?
options: Where the waters meet the sea
questions.explain: Iroquoian guides used kanata for the village of Stadacona, and Cartier extended it to the whole surrounding region.

questions.q: On his 1535 voyage, Cartier visited Hochelaga, a fortified Iroquoian town on the site of which present-day city?
questions.explain: Cartier climbed the hill he named Mont Royal; Stadacona, the other town he visited, stood where Quebec City is now.

questions.q: In 1605, French colonists led by Pierre Dugua de Mons and Samuel de Champlain founded Port-Royal in which region?
questions.explain: After a deadly winter on St. Croix Island, the colonists moved across the Bay of Fundy to Port-Royal, an early center of French Acadia.

questions.q: Which English sea captain completed the first English voyage around the world, from 1577 to 1580?
questions.explain: Drake raided Spanish ports and ships along the Pacific coast on the way, and Queen Elizabeth I knighted him aboard the Golden Hind in 1581.

questions.q: In the 1560s John Hawkins became known as the first English captain to do what?
options: Ship enslaved Africans across the Atlantic for sale
questions.explain: Hawkins seized Africans in Sierra Leone and sold them in the Spanish Caribbean; his 1568 defeat at San Juan de Ulua soured England's ties with Spain.

questions.q: Virginia Dare, born at Roanoke in 1587, is remembered as what?
options: The first child born to English parents in the Americas
The first Englishwoman to sail across the Atlantic to America
questions.explain: Virginia was the granddaughter of Governor John White; she vanished with the rest of the colonists before White returned in 1590.

questions.q: Manteo, a Croatoan man who traveled to England and back, played what role in the Roanoke ventures?
options: He led the attack that destroyed the colony
He served as an interpreter and ally of the English
He guided Spanish soldiers to the island
questions.explain: Manteo sailed to England in 1584, helped Harriot learn his language and was baptized by the colonists in 1587.

questions.q: In 1488 the Portuguese captain Bartolomeu Dias became the first European known to sail around which point?
questions.explain: Dias's voyage proved a sea route around Africa to the Indian Ocean existed, opening the way for Vasco da Gama's 1497-1499 trip to India.

questions.q: Which Portuguese commander, sailing for India in 1500, reached the coast of Brazil and claimed it for Portugal?
questions.explain: Cabral swung far west into the Atlantic and sighted Brazil in April 1500, then continued on to India.

questions.q: The Treaty of Tordesillas set the dividing line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. Which later Portuguese colony lay east of that line?
questions.explain: Because the bulge of South America crossed the line, Portugal could claim Brazil while Spain claimed most of the rest of the Americas.

questions.q: After the Santa Maria ran aground on Christmas Eve 1492, Columbus left about 39 men in a fort on Hispaniola called what?
questions.explain: When Columbus returned in 1493 he found the fort burned and all the men dead, apparently after conflict with the Taino.

questions.q: Founded in 1496 on Hispaniola, which city is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded settlement in the Americas?
questions.explain: Bartholomew Columbus founded the city, which became the first seat of Spanish rule in the Americas; it is now the capital of the Dominican Republic.

questions.q: Which English word comes from the Taino language of the Caribbean?
questions.explain: Spanish borrowed huracan from the Taino; canoe, hammock and barbecue also trace back to Taino words, while moccasin and tomahawk are Algonquian.

questions.q: The Laws of Burgos (1512) are significant as Spain's first attempt to do what?
options: Regulate how colonists treated Native workers in the Americas
Divide the world's new lands with Portugal
Ban the import of enslaved Africans
questions.explain: The laws, a response to Dominican protests, limited hours and punishments for Native laborers, though they were widely ignored.

questions.q: Pope Paul III's 1537 bull Sublimis Deus declared what about the Native peoples of the Americas?
options: They were subjects of the Portuguese crown
They were rational people who must not be enslaved
They could be required to work in the mines
They owed the church a yearly tithe of gold
questions.explain: The bull affirmed that Indigenous peoples could receive the faith and keep their liberty and property, though enforcement in the colonies was weak.

questions.q: From 1524, which body in Spain governed the American colonies on the king's behalf?
questions.explain: The council drafted laws, named officials and heard appeals for Spanish America; audiencias were courts in the colonies that answered to it.

questions.q: Bartolome de las Casas's 1552 book about Spanish cruelty in the Americas was titled what?
options: The True History of the Conquest of New Spain
The Royal Commentaries of the Incas and General History of Peru
A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies
The General History of the Things of New Spain
questions.explain: Rivals of Spain translated and reprinted the book widely, feeding the Black Legend; the other titles are by Sahagun, Diaz del Castillo and Garcilaso.

questions.q: Early in his career, Las Casas proposed relieving Native laborers by bringing in whom, a proposal he later regretted?
questions.explain: Las Casas later wrote that enslaving Africans was just as unjust as enslaving Native Americans and repented his earlier advice.

questions.q: In 1562 at Mani, in the Yucatan, Bishop Diego de Landa ordered the burning of what?
questions.explain: Landa destroyed dozens of Maya codices; only four pre-conquest Maya books are known to survive today.

questions.q: Which historian coined the term 'Columbian Exchange' in a 1972 book?
questions.explain: Crosby's The Columbian Exchange traced how plants, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic after 1492 and reshaped both hemispheres.

questions.q: Which two mosquito-borne diseases reached the Americas from the Eastern Hemisphere after 1492, later shaping life in tropical and southern lowlands?
questions.explain: Both diseases came with ships and the slave trade; they took a heavy toll in the Caribbean and low country, where mosquitoes thrived.

questions.q: After 1492, which American crops helped feed rapid population growth in China?
questions.explain: Maize and sweet potatoes grew on hillsides and poor soils unsuited to rice, letting Chinese farmers expand into new land.

questions.q: Chili peppers, now central to cooking in India, Thailand and Korea, originated where?
questions.explain: Portuguese and Spanish traders spread chili peppers from the Americas across Africa and Asia within decades of Columbus's voyages.

questions.q: Enriquillo led a long Taino rebellion against Spanish rule in the 1520s and early 1530s on which island?
questions.explain: Enriquillo held out in the Bahoruco Mountains until 1533, when he won a treaty granting his followers their freedom.

questions.q: In Spanish America, communities formed by people who escaped slavery, such as the one led by Gaspar Yanga near Veracruz, were often called what?
questions.explain: After years of resistance, Yanga's community won Spanish recognition as a free town in the early 1600s.

questions.q: Around the year 1000, Norse sailors built a short-lived settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows on which island?
questions.explain: Excavated in the 1960s, the site is the only confirmed Norse settlement in North America and matches sagas about a land called Vinland.

questions.q: Which language of the Mexica gave English words such as tomato, avocado and coyote?
questions.explain: Spanish borrowed tomatl, ahuacatl and coyotl from Nahuatl, and English took them from Spanish.

questions.q: Why did the Spanish conquest of the Maya take far longer than the conquest of the Aztecs?
options: The Maya were divided among many independent states, not one empire
The Maya had acquired steel weapons and cannon from Portuguese traders
The Maya lived on islands Spain could not reach
questions.explain: With no single capital to seize, the Spanish had to subdue Maya states one by one; the last independent kingdom fell in 1697.

questions.q: What was the name of the royal road that linked Mexico City to the new Spanish settlements in New Mexico from 1598?
options: El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro
questions.explain: The road ran some 1,500 miles; caravans carried goods, settlers and missionaries north and hides and wool south for over two centuries.

questions.q: After the expedition's commander was killed in the Philippines in 1521, which navigator brought the surviving ship, the Victoria, home to Spain to complete the first voyage around the world?
questions.explain: Magellan died at Mactan; Elcano reached Spain in September 1522 with 18 survivors.

questions.q: In colonial Spanish America, people of Spanish descent born in the Americas were called what?
questions.explain: Criollos often owned land and wealth but were usually passed over for the top offices, which went to Spain-born peninsulares.

questions.q: How many voyages did Christopher Columbus make to the Americas?
questions.explain: Columbus sailed in 1492, 1493, 1498 and 1502; on the last two he reached the coasts of South and Central America.

questions.q: By about what time had most people left Cahokia, once the largest city north of Mexico?
questions.explain: Cahokia peaked around 1050 to 1150; flooding, drought, resource strain and conflict are among the explanations for its decline.

questions.q: Mississippian societies of the Southeast and Midwest were typically organized as what?
options: Chiefdoms ruled by hereditary elites from mound centers
Empires governed by written law codes
Small egalitarian bands of mobile foragers with no fixed towns
questions.explain: Chiefs lived atop platform mounds and collected tribute of food and goods; de Soto met such chiefdoms, including Coosa, in the 1540s.

questions.q: After about 1300, as the Four Corners region emptied, many Ancestral Puebloans moved where?
options: To the Rio Grande valley and the Hopi and Zuni areas
To the Gulf coast of Texas
questions.explain: Their descendants include the Pueblo peoples of the Rio Grande, Hopi and Zuni, whom the Spanish met in the 1500s.

questions.q: The Navajo and Apache speak Athabaskan languages. Where do linguists and archaeologists believe their ancestors migrated from?
options: The subarctic of western Canada and Alaska
The Valley of Mexico and the Gulf coast of Mesoamerica
questions.explain: Related Athabaskan languages are spoken in Alaska and northwest Canada; the ancestors of the Navajo and Apache reached the Southwest around 1400 or later.

questions.q: When Champlain sailed up the St. Lawrence in 1603, what had happened to the Iroquoian towns Cartier visited in the 1530s?
options: They had become the Huron capital
They had been conquered by Spain
They had vanished, for reasons still debated
They had grown into French trading posts
questions.explain: Warfare with the Mohawk or other Haudenosaunee, European diseases and migration are among proposed explanations for the disappearance of the St. Lawrence Iroquoians.

questions.q: The Apalachee people, whose name was later given to the Appalachian Mountains, lived in which region?
questions.explain: Narvaez's men recorded the name in 1528; mapmakers later applied it to the mountains far to the north.

questions.q: Columbus's second voyage in 1493 differed from his first mainly because it did what?
options: Reached the mainland coast of North America near Florida and the Carolinas
Brought more than a thousand settlers and livestock to colonize Hispaniola
Returned with the first cargo of silver
Sailed around the southern tip of Africa
questions.explain: Seventeen ships carried colonists, horses, pigs, cattle and seeds, beginning the transfer of European farming to the Americas.

questions.q: During the 1892 Homestead strike, anarchist Alexander Berkman tried to assassinate which Carnegie Steel executive?
questions.explain: Frick survived being shot and stabbed; the attack turned public sympathy away from the strikers.

questions.q: In 1893 the governor of Illinois drew national criticism for doing what?
options: Ordering the arrest of anarchist newspaper editors
Calling out the militia against Pullman strikers
Pardoning three surviving men convicted in the Haymarket case
questions.explain: Governor John Peter Altgeld concluded the Haymarket trial had been unfair; the pardons of Fielden, Neebe and Schwab cost him politically.

questions.q: The Knights of Labor began in 1869 as a secret society of which workers in Philadelphia?
questions.explain: Uriah Stephens and fellow tailors founded the order; it dropped its secrecy in 1881 and grew rapidly under Terence Powderly.

questions.q: In September 1869, Jay Gould and Jim Fisk tried to corner the market in what, causing the 'Black Friday' panic?
questions.explain: The scheme collapsed when President Grant had the Treasury sell $4 million in gold, crashing the price on September 24.

questions.q: In 1882 Rockefeller and his partners organized Standard Oil as a trust. What did this arrangement do?
options: Made every refinery worker a part owner
Let a board of trustees control many companies' stock as one unit
Made the firm a government-chartered monopoly partly owned by Ohio
Split the firm into regional competitors
questions.explain: Stockholders in about 40 companies traded their shares for trust certificates, letting nine trustees run the whole empire.

questions.q: In 1882, Thomas Edison opened which pioneering central electric power station in Lower Manhattan?
questions.explain: Pearl Street began serving about 85 customers in September 1882 using direct current, the model for central power plants.

questions.q: Red Cloud's War (1866-1868) ended with the United States agreeing to do what?
options: Abandon its forts along the Bozeman Trail
Move the Lakota to Indian Territory
Buy the Black Hills from the Lakota
Pay for a railroad across Lakota land
questions.explain: The 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty closed the forts guarding the trail to Montana's gold fields, a rare victory for a Native nation over the Army.

questions.q: In the Modoc War of 1872-1873, Kintpuash (Captain Jack) and a small band held out for months in which terrain on the California-Oregon border?
options: The lava beds near Tule Lake
questions.explain: The Modoc used lava caves and trenches as natural forts; General Edward Canby was killed during peace talks, and Kintpuash was hanged.

questions.q: An 1871 Indian Appropriations Act changed federal Indian policy by doing what?
options: Creating the Bureau of Indian Affairs
Dividing reservations into individual family allotments of 160 acres
Ending the practice of making treaties with Native nations
Granting citizenship to all Native Americans
questions.explain: The House, left out of Senate-ratified treaties, insisted that tribes no longer be treated as nations; later policy came through laws and executive orders.

questions.q: President Grant's 'Peace Policy' of 1869 did what?
options: Gave church groups such as the Quakers a role in running Indian agencies
Banned settlers from crossing the Mississippi
Recognized Native nations as foreign countries
questions.explain: Religious denominations nominated agents to replace corrupt political appointees, though Army campaigns continued alongside the policy.

questions.q: Which Army officer, founder of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, summed up its aim as 'Kill the Indian in him, and save the man'?
questions.explain: Pratt spoke the line in 1892; Carlisle cut students' hair, banned Native languages and became a model for boarding schools nationwide.

questions.q: The Ghost Dance of 1889-1890 spread from the visions of Wovoka, a prophet of which people?
questions.explain: Wovoka, of Nevada, taught that dancing and right living would bring renewal; Lakota followers' version alarmed officials before Wounded Knee.

questions.q: Which formerly enslaved man from Tennessee promoted Black migration to Kansas in the 1870s and was called the 'Father of the Exodus'?
questions.explain: Singleton organized settlement colonies and circulated flyers urging Black Southerners to seek land and safety in Kansas.

questions.q: Which Agriculture Department clerk founded the Patrons of Husbandry, or Grange, in 1867?
questions.explain: Kelley toured the war-torn South for the department in 1866 and decided farmers needed a national organization; the Grange was founded in Washington in December 1867.

questions.q: Who was the People's Party's presidential candidate in 1892, winning more than a million votes and 22 electoral votes?
questions.explain: Weaver, an Iowa Civil War general, had also run for the Greenback Party in 1880; he carried Kansas, Colorado, Idaho and Nevada.

questions.q: William H. Harvey's best-selling 1894 pamphlet Coin's Financial School argued for what?
options: Unlimited coinage of silver at 16 to 1
A new national bank modeled on Alexander Hamilton's
questions.explain: In the book a boy named Coin bested bankers and professors in debate; it helped build the free-silver movement before 1896.

questions.q: During the 1890s, Treasury officials and investors watched which symbolic minimum level of the gold reserve backing U.S. currency?
questions.explain: When the reserve fell below $100 million in 1893, confidence collapsed; by early 1895 it had fallen near $41 million before Morgan's syndicate stepped in.

questions.q: Mississippi's 1890 constitution became a model for disfranchising Black voters by requiring what?
options: Proof of service in the Union army
Three generations of residence in the state
A poll tax and a literacy test judged by local officials
questions.explain: Registrars could pass white voters under an 'understanding clause' while rejecting Black voters; other Southern states copied the plan.

questions.q: Louisiana's 1898 constitution exempted men from literacy and property tests if their fathers or grandfathers could vote before 1867. What was this called?
questions.explain: The 1867 cutoff excluded virtually all Black men; the Supreme Court struck down such clauses in Guinn v. United States (1915).

questions.q: Which phrase, spoken by a Protestant minister backing James G. Blaine in 1884, may have cost Blaine New York and the presidency?
options: Burn this letter, kind regards to Mrs. Fisher
questions.explain: Rev. Samuel Burchard called the Democrats the party of 'Rum, Romanism, and Rebellion'; Irish Catholic voters took offense and Cleveland narrowly won New York.

questions.q: Which New York senator, who resigned in 1881 in a patronage fight with President Garfield, led the Republican faction that defended the spoils system?
questions.explain: Conkling and fellow senator Thomas Platt quit over Garfield's choice for collector of the Port of New York, expecting reelection; the legislature refused.

questions.q: In 1894, Cleveland let which tariff become law without his signature, denouncing its many protectionist amendments as 'party perfidy and party dishonor'?
questions.explain: The House's tariff cuts were gutted by hundreds of Senate amendments; the law also carried an income tax later struck down by the Supreme Court.

questions.q: Secretary of State James G. Blaine hosted the first International Conference of American States in 1889-1890. Which organization grew out of it?
questions.explain: The conference created a Commercial Bureau of the American Republics, renamed the Pan American Union in 1910; its headquarters stands near the White House.

questions.q: In the 1895 Venezuela boundary dispute, Secretary of State Richard Olney asserted U.S. power in the hemisphere against which country?
questions.explain: Olney claimed that the United States was 'practically sovereign' in the hemisphere; Britain agreed to arbitration over British Guiana's border.

questions.q: In 1889, a standoff among American, German and British warships over which Pacific islands ended when a cyclone wrecked most of the ships?
questions.explain: The storm at Apia sank or beached six warships; the powers then agreed to share control and in 1899 divided the islands.

questions.q: The 1887 'Bayonet Constitution,' forced on King Kalakaua by mostly American businessmen, did what?
options: Cut the king's powers, denied Asians the vote and set wealth tests for voters
Banned foreign ownership of sugar land
questions.explain: Armed members of the Hawaiian League imposed property and income requirements for voting, putting power in the hands of wealthy planters.

questions.q: When the U.S.-Hawaii trade reciprocity treaty was renewed in 1887, what did the United States gain?
options: Exclusive rights to a naval station at Pearl Harbor
questions.explain: Duty-free sugar exports had made planters rich since 1875; the renewal gave the U.S. Navy the harbor that later became its Pacific base.

questions.q: After the 1893 overthrow of Hawaii's monarchy, what did President Cleveland do with the treaty to annex the islands?
options: Signed it and sent troops to occupy Honolulu
Submitted it to a vote of all Hawaiians
Traded it to Britain for rights in Samoa
Withdrew it from the Senate and ordered an inquiry, which found U.S. officials had aided the coup
questions.explain: James Blount's report concluded that U.S. minister John Stevens and landed Marines helped topple Queen Liliuokalani; annexation waited until 1898.

questions.q: In 1898 Hawaii was annexed by what means, after an annexation treaty failed to win two-thirds of the Senate?
options: A popular vote of Hawaii's residents
questions.explain: The Newlands Resolution needed only simple majorities in both houses; McKinley signed it in July 1898 amid the war with Spain.

questions.q: The 1898 de Lome letter, published by Hearst's New York Journal, angered Americans because the Spanish minister called whom weak?
questions.explain: Enrique Dupuy de Lome called McKinley 'weak and a bidder for the admiration of the crowd'; the Maine exploded less than a week after publication.

questions.q: Spanish general Valeriano Weyler, called 'the Butcher' in the American press, fought Cuban rebels by doing what?
options: Forcing rural Cubans into fortified camps where many died
Freeing enslaved Cubans to join his army
questions.explain: Weyler's reconcentration policy herded hundreds of thousands into camps with little food; disease killed huge numbers and outraged Americans.

questions.q: Under the 1898 Treaty of Paris, the United States agreed to pay Spain how much in connection with the Philippines?
questions.explain: The payment accompanied Spain's cession of the Philippines; $7.2 million was the price of Alaska and $15 million went to Mexico in 1848.

questions.q: Founded in 1871 near deposits of iron ore, coal and limestone, which city became the iron and steel center of the New South?
questions.explain: Birmingham grew so fast it was called the Magic City; its mills relied heavily on Black workers, including convict laborers.

questions.q: In the 1880s and 1890s, cotton textile mills spread across which Southern region, drawing poor white families into mill villages?
options: The Piedmont of the Carolinas and Georgia
questions.explain: Water power from Piedmont rivers and cheap labor drew mills; families often worked together, children included, and lived in company housing.

questions.q: Which Chicago architect, designer of the Wainwright Building, wrote that 'form ever follows function'?
questions.explain: Sullivan's 1896 essay on the tall office building shaped modern architecture; Frank Lloyd Wright worked for him as a young draftsman.

questions.q: Emma Lazarus wrote her sonnet 'The New Colossus' in 1883 to raise money for what?
options: The pedestal of the Statue of Liberty
A shelter for Jewish refugees in New York
questions.explain: The poem, with its 'huddled masses yearning to breathe free,' was put on a plaque inside the pedestal in 1903.

questions.q: In 1897 President Cleveland vetoed a bill backed by the Immigration Restriction League that would have required immigrants to do what?
questions.explain: Cleveland called the test a radical departure from national policy; Congress finally imposed one over Wilson's veto in 1917.

questions.q: Which Christian group, founded in London by William and Catherine Booth, began organized work in the United States in 1880?
questions.explain: Its uniformed officers held street meetings and ran shelters in the slums; the Volunteers of America was a later offshoot founded in the U.S. in 1896.

questions.q: In 1879 Belva Lockwood became the first woman to do what?
options: Be appointed to a president's cabinet as a department head
Practice law before the U.S. Supreme Court
questions.explain: Lockwood lobbied Congress to pass a law letting women argue before the Court; she later ran for president in 1884 and 1888.

questions.q: In Minor v. Happersett (1875), the Supreme Court ruled what?
options: States could not bar women from practicing law
Citizenship did not give women a constitutional right to vote
Married women had a right to own property
Women could serve on federal juries
questions.explain: Virginia Minor argued the Fourteenth Amendment protected her vote; the unanimous ruling pushed suffragists toward a constitutional amendment.

questions.q: The Comstock Act of 1873 made it a federal crime to do what?
options: Employ children under twelve in factories
Mail obscene material, including information on contraception
questions.explain: Anthony Comstock lobbied for the law and enforced it as a postal inspector for decades.

questions.q: In November 1889, which four states were admitted to the Union within about ten days of one another?
options: North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana and Washington
Arizona, New Mexico, Oklahoma and Utah
questions.explain: Republicans in Congress welcomed the new, mostly Republican states; Idaho and Wyoming followed in July 1890.

questions.q: In Strauder v. West Virginia (1880), the Supreme Court struck down a state law that did what?
options: Required separate railroad cars by race
Barred Black men from serving on juries
Imposed a poll tax on voters
questions.explain: The Court held that excluding Black citizens from juries by law violated equal protection, though other methods of exclusion soon spread.

questions.q: In Allgeyer v. Louisiana (1897), the Supreme Court for the first time read which right into the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause?
questions.explain: The doctrine became the basis for striking down many labor laws in the Lochner era, until the Court abandoned it in 1937.

questions.q: In Juilliard v. Greenman (1884), the Supreme Court upheld Congress's power to do what?
options: Set railroad rates in every state
Make paper money legal tender even in peacetime
questions.explain: The Legal Tender Cases had upheld greenbacks as a wartime measure; Juilliard extended the power to peacetime.

questions.q: In 1878 Rutherford B. Hayes began which White House tradition after Congress barred children from playing on the Capitol grounds?
options: The Fourth of July fireworks picnic
questions.explain: Children who had rolled eggs on the Capitol lawn were invited to the White House South Lawn, and the event became an annual custom.

questions.q: Which president was the first to have electric lighting installed in the White House, in 1891?
questions.explain: The Harrisons were reportedly so wary of the switches that they sometimes left the lights on all night rather than touch them.

questions.q: In 1887 Cleveland vetoed the Texas Seed Bill, which would have given drought-stricken farmers what?
questions.explain: Cleveland wrote that 'though the people support the Government, the Government should not support the people.'

questions.q: By the 1890s, critics mocked the U.S. Senate with what nickname because of its many wealthy members tied to big business?
questions.explain: Chosen by state legislatures, many senators owed their seats to corporate allies, a key argument for the Seventeenth Amendment.

questions.q: Between 1850 and 1871, Congress granted railroads roughly how much public land?
questions.explain: Federal grants of about 131 million acres, plus state grants, helped finance western lines; Congress stopped making new grants in 1871.

questions.q: Which leader of California's Workingmen's Party in the late 1870s rallied crowds with the slogan 'The Chinese must go!'?
questions.explain: Kearney, an Irish immigrant drayman, led sandlot rallies in San Francisco; the party helped write anti-Chinese clauses into California's 1879 constitution.

questions.q: In 1871, a mob killed about 18 Chinese residents in which city, one of the deadliest mass lynchings in U.S. history?
questions.explain: The massacre in the city's Chinatown followed a shootout that killed a white man; few of the attackers were punished.

questions.q: In the 1897 Lattimer massacre in Pennsylvania, sheriff's deputies shot unarmed striking coal miners who were mostly what?
options: Black migrants from the Deep South hired as strikebreakers
questions.explain: Nineteen marchers were killed, many shot in the back; the deputies were tried and acquitted.

questions.q: By the 1890 census, which city had passed Philadelphia to become the second largest in the United States?
questions.explain: Chicago topped a million people in 1890, growing from about 30,000 in 1850 as a rail, meatpacking and grain hub.

questions.q: Alexander 'Boss' Shepherd paved streets and laid sewers in the early 1870s as the dominant member (vice-chair) of the Board of Public Works and later governor of which city's territorial government?
questions.explain: Shepherd's projects modernized the capital but ran up huge debts; Congress abolished the territorial government in 1874 and put appointed commissioners in charge.

questions.q: Which Smithsonian building on the National Mall opened in 1881 as the U.S. National Museum, showing objects from the 1876 Centennial Exhibition?
questions.explain: Railcar loads of Centennial exhibits donated to the Smithsonian needed a home; the building hosted President Garfield's inaugural ball in 1881.

questions.q: Settlers who slipped into Oklahoma's Unassigned Lands before the official start of the 1889 land run were called what?
questions.explain: Boomers had lobbied to open the land; Sooners jumped the gun, and the name later became the University of Oklahoma's nickname.

questions.q: The Klondike gold rush of 1896-1899 drew prospectors to which region?
options: Canada's Yukon, by way of Alaska
Colorado's Pikes Peak and Cripple Creek districts
questions.explain: About 100,000 people set out; most traveled through Alaska ports like Skagway and climbed passes such as the Chilkoot.

questions.q: Which Illinois livestock dealer built stockyards beside the Kansas Pacific Railway in 1867, creating the first great cow town at the end of the Chisholm Trail?
questions.explain: McCoy's yards let Texas drovers sell cattle for shipment to Chicago; the phrase 'the real McCoy' is sometimes linked to him.

questions.q: Which Northern Paiute author and activist wrote Life Among the Piutes (1883)?
questions.explain: Winnemucca's book, an early autobiography by a Native American woman, attacked corrupt agents and the forced removal of her people.

questions.q: In 1710 nearly 3,000 German Palatine refugees were sent by the British government to which colony to make tar and pitch for the navy?
questions.explain: The naval stores camps on the Hudson failed; many Palatines moved to the Schoharie and Mohawk valleys or on to Pennsylvania.

questions.q: By the early 1700s, South Carolina became the first mainland English colony to have what?
options: A majority of people of African descent
A population made up mostly of German-speaking immigrants
questions.explain: Rice planting drove huge imports of enslaved Africans; by about 1708 they outnumbered whites, and fears of revolt shaped the colony's laws.

questions.q: An epidemic from about 1616 to 1619 had what effect on the New England coast before the Pilgrims arrived?
options: It wiped out English fishing camps
It destroyed the region's maize crops
It drove the Wampanoag inland to the Great Lakes
It killed a large share of the coastal Native population
questions.explain: The Pilgrims settled on cleared fields of Patuxet, a Wampanoag town emptied by the disease; Tisquantum (Squanto) had been born there.

questions.q: Settlers of New Sweden, founded on the Delaware River in 1638, are credited with bringing what to North America?
questions.explain: Swedish and Finnish colonists built notched-log houses familiar from home; the style later spread across the American frontier.

questions.q: To clear land quickly, many colonial farmers girdled trees. What did that involve?
options: Cutting a ring through the bark so the tree died standing
Pulling trees down with teams of oxen
Bending and weaving young saplings together to form living fences
questions.explain: Farmers planted corn among the dead trunks, a method colonists learned partly from Native practice; the trees were felled or burned later.

questions.q: Wealthy Lowcountry rice planters often left their plantations for Charleston or the mountains in summer. Why?
options: To escape malaria and other fevers in the swampy rice districts
To avoid winter flooding of the fields
To sell their rice crops in person to merchants in London
questions.explain: Flooded rice fields bred mosquitoes; planters left enslaved workers, many with some inherited resistance, behind with overseers.

questions.q: Which fish, dried and salted, became New England's leading export in the 1600s and 1700s?
questions.explain: Massachusetts hung a carved 'Sacred Cod' in its State House; the best fish went to Catholic Europe and the poorest to Caribbean plantations.

questions.q: Of the enslaved Africans who survived the Atlantic crossing, roughly what share were brought to mainland British North America?
questions.explain: Most went to Brazil and the Caribbean; about 400,000 reached mainland North America, where the enslaved population grew mainly through births.

questions.q: Which Missouri trader opened the Santa Fe Trail in 1821, returning from New Mexico with a large profit?
questions.explain: Becknell is called the father of the Santa Fe Trail; his 1822 trip proved wagons could cross the route.

questions.q: After white mobs attacked Black neighborhoods in Cincinnati in 1829, hundreds of Black residents left to found the Wilberforce settlement where?
questions.explain: Ohio began enforcing its Black Laws, which required a bond of $500; the riots that followed drove many families across the border to present-day Ontario.

questions.q: In 1834 an anti-Catholic mob burned an Ursuline convent in which Massachusetts town?
questions.explain: Rumors that a woman was held against her will fed the attack; the convent school mainly educated daughters of Protestant families.

questions.q: Before he became a fire-eating secessionist, Edmund Ruffin was known for promoting what?
options: Restoring worn-out Southern soil with marl
Breeding mules for the cotton belt
questions.explain: Ruffin's 1832 Essay on Calcareous Manures showed farmers how to fix acidic, exhausted soil; he later fired an early shot at Fort Sumter.

questions.q: John James Audubon's The Birds of America, published between 1827 and 1838, was notable for what?
options: Maps of the Lewis and Clark route
The first scientific system for naming plants
Life-size color prints of North American birds
Early photographs of western wildlife taken on government surveys
questions.explain: The giant 'double elephant folio' had 435 hand-colored plates; the Library of Congress holds a set.

questions.q: Thomas Cole's 1836 painting The Oxbow contrasts what?
options: Stormy wilderness and cultivated farmland along the Connecticut River
Ocean storms and a calm harbor
questions.explain: Cole painted himself in the wild foreground; the view from Mount Holyoke raised questions about how settlement was changing the land.

questions.q: Many Irish immigrants of the 1820s and 1830s found work doing what?
options: Crewing whaling ships out of Nantucket and New Bedford
questions.explain: Irish laborers worked on the Erie Canal and dug many other canals and railroads, often for low pay in dangerous conditions.

questions.q: In 1812, the Russian-American Company built which outpost on the northern California coast?
questions.explain: Russians and Alaska Native hunters used it to hunt sea otters and grow food for Alaska; John Sutter bought its goods in 1841.

questions.q: Johnny Appleseed, whose real name was John Chapman, planted apple nurseries mainly in which region?
questions.explain: Chapman started nurseries ahead of settlers and sold seedlings to them; he died in Indiana in 1845.

questions.q: During the Second Seminole War, many Seminoles held out against the Army by retreating into which region?
questions.explain: The swamps hid Seminole and Black Seminole fighters; the war cost the U.S. Army about 1,500 lives and never fully ended with a treaty.

questions.q: According to Census Bureau estimates, in which year did the U.S. population pass 300 million?
questions.explain: The 300 million mark came in October 2006, about 39 years after the population passed 200 million in 1967.

questions.q: A 2012 Pew study found that by 2010, which group had passed Hispanics as the largest share of new immigrants to the United States?
questions.explain: Pew found that 36 percent of new immigrants in 2010 were Asian, as Mexican migration slowed during the recession.

questions.q: Pew research in 2012 found that net migration from Mexico to the United States between 2005 and 2010 had fallen to about what level?
questions.explain: The housing bust, tighter enforcement and falling birth rates in Mexico ended four decades of heavy net migration.

questions.q: Operation Gatekeeper, launched in 1994, tightened border enforcement in which area, pushing many crossers toward deserts and mountains?
questions.explain: Fencing and agents in the San Diego sector cut crossings there but shifted them east, and deaths in remote areas rose.

questions.q: Which temporary visa for workers in 'specialty occupations,' given its modern form by the Immigration Act of 1990, became heavily used by technology companies?
questions.explain: The 1990 law set an annual H-1B cap of 65,000; the K-1 is a fiance visa and the bracero program ended in 1964.

questions.q: In 2003, the functions of which agency were divided among new federal bureaus, including ICE, CBP and USCIS?
questions.explain: The INS, part of the Justice Department since 1940, was abolished when the Department of Homeland Security took over; FEMA moved in intact.

questions.q: California voters' Proposition 227 in 1998 sharply limited what in public schools?
questions.explain: The measure required most English learners to be taught in English; voters largely repealed it in 2016.

questions.q: Which metropolitan area became home to the largest Somali community in the United States after refugees began arriving in the 1990s?
questions.explain: Refugees fleeing Somalia's civil war were resettled there, and many relatives followed; Minnesota later elected Somali American officials.

questions.q: Which Michigan city, next to Detroit, has one of the largest concentrations of Arab Americans in the United States?
questions.explain: Arab immigrants were first drawn to Ford's auto plants in the early 1900s; Lebanese, Yemeni and Iraqi families arrived later.

questions.q: In 2014, a surge of unaccompanied children arriving at the southern border came mostly from which countries?
options: Cuba, Haiti and the Dominican Republic
questions.explain: Gang violence and poverty in Central America's Northern Triangle drove tens of thousands of minors north, straining shelters and courts.

questions.q: In 2000, federal agents took six-year-old Elian Gonzalez from relatives in Miami so he could return with his father to which country?
questions.explain: Elian survived a boat sinking that killed his mother; the custody fight became a national drama before courts sided with his father.

questions.q: Since about 1970, and especially after 1990, Black Americans' net migration has moved in what direction?
options: Out of the country to the Caribbean
Toward the South, reversing the earlier Great Migration
Toward small towns in New England
questions.explain: Demographers call it the New Great Migration; metro Atlanta, Houston and Dallas drew large numbers of Black newcomers.

questions.q: Which state grew fastest in percentage terms in both the 2000 and 2010 censuses, driven by the growth of Las Vegas?
questions.explain: Nevada grew about 66 percent in the 1990s and 35 percent in the 2000s, the fastest of any state both times.

questions.q: The Great Flood of 1993 caused massive damage along which rivers?
questions.explain: Months of heavy rain broke hundreds of levees across nine Midwestern states, and many towns later moved buildings out of the floodplain.

questions.q: The 1988 Yellowstone fires, which burned roughly a third of the park, set off a national debate over what policy?
questions.explain: Under a policy since 1972, many lightning fires were allowed to burn; scientists later found the forests regrew vigorously.

questions.q: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act included a provision to open part of which protected area to oil and gas leasing?
options: The Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness
questions.explain: Opening the refuge's coastal plain had been debated for decades; its first lease sale in 2021 drew few bids.

questions.q: In West Virginia v. EPA (2022), the Supreme Court limited the EPA's power to do what?
options: Force a shift of power generation away from coal plants
questions.explain: Citing the 'major questions' doctrine, the Court said Congress had not clearly authorized such sweeping, industry-wide emissions rules.

questions.q: After the United States formally left the Paris climate agreement in November 2020, when did it rejoin?
questions.explain: Joe Biden signed the order to rejoin on his first day in office, and the return took effect 30 days later.

questions.q: In August 2021 the federal government declared its first-ever shortage on the lower Colorado River, triggered by low water in which reservoir?
questions.explain: A long drought drained the reservoir behind Hoover Dam; Arizona took the largest cut in deliveries in 2022.

questions.q: Hurricane Sandy in 2012 caused its worst damage in which area?
questions.explain: Its storm surge flooded lower Manhattan and the subways and wrecked large stretches of the Jersey Shore.

questions.q: In 1843 the first large wagon train, about a thousand people, set out from Missouri in what became known as the Great Emigration. Where were most headed?
questions.explain: Guided part of the way by Marcus Whitman, the train proved families with wagons could cross to Oregon, and thousands followed each year.

questions.q: In an 1824 treaty with the United States, Russia agreed not to claim land on the Pacific coast south of what latitude?
questions.explain: The line later marked the southern tip of Alaska and became the 'Fifty-four forty' rallying cry for claiming all of Oregon in the 1840s.

questions.q: After Mexico secularized the California missions in the 1830s, much of the mission land ended up as what?
options: U.S. Army forts and supply depots
Large ranchos granted mostly to Californio families
questions.explain: Mission Indians were promised land but received little; ranchos raising cattle for hides and tallow came to dominate Mexican California.

questions.q: In the late 1940s and 1950s, cheap airfares and Puerto Rico's shift from farming to factories helped drive a large migration of Puerto Ricans mainly to which city?
questions.explain: Puerto Ricans were U.S. citizens and could move freely; by 1960 hundreds of thousands lived in New York neighborhoods such as East Harlem.

questions.q: In February 2021, a severe winter storm caused massive power failures in which state, whose electric grid is largely separate from the rest of the country?
questions.explain: Frozen equipment knocked out generation across the ERCOT grid, leaving millions without power for days; hundreds of deaths were linked to the storm.

questions.q: The Cuban Adjustment Act of 1966 gave Cubans who reached the United States what special benefit?
options: The chance to apply for permanent residence after a period in the U.S.
questions.explain: The law, passed during the Cold War, let Cuban parolees become legal permanent residents without the usual immigrant visa process.

questions.q: Which insect pest spread from Mexico into Texas in the 1890s and across the Cotton Belt by the 1920s, pushing many farmers off the land?
questions.explain: The weevil destroyed cotton bolls, ruining many tenant farmers; the damage pushed Southern farmers to diversify and added to migration north.

questions.q: The Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971 resolved Native land claims by creating what?
options: A trust fund paid out to each person once
Regional and village Native corporations that received land and money
Reservations run by the Bureau of Indian Affairs
questions.explain: Alaska Natives received about 44 million acres and nearly $1 billion, clearing the way for the oil pipeline from Prudhoe Bay.

questions.q: The Trans-Alaska Pipeline, finished in 1977, carries oil from Prudhoe Bay on the Arctic coast to which port?
questions.explain: The 800-mile line crosses three mountain ranges and permafrost; the 1973 oil crisis helped push its approval through Congress.
